name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,757

clue.text: Pneumatic model excited clean-cut boys

indicators.note: excited things jump about, so the letters of the boys that follow are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters with the hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: A glamour shoot in which a curvy model gets the neat young men worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pneumatic model' is steered to mean a buxom woman; here pneumatic just means filled with air, and the model is a toy fortress. A bouncy castle is an inflatable play structure for children.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflatable castle-shaped play structure is literally a blown-up replica of a fortress, so an air-filled model describes it plainly.

clue.text: In the sack, soldiers make babies

indicators.note: the soldiers are in the sack, so they are placed inside the word for bed

blocks.note: the sack is slang for bed, as in hitting the sack
RE = Royal Engineers, the army corps

explanation.surface: A cheeky line about troops getting busy between the sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface places the soldiers in bed; the wordplay does exactly that, putting the engineers inside the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To breed is to produce offspring, a plain verb synonym for reproducing or having young.

clue.text: Brazen hand abuse must be rectified!

indicators.note: rectifying something puts it right, so the letters of the hand abuse have to be rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A shameless moral warning that a solitary vice needs correcting.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a nudge-nudge joke about self-abuse; the definition sits at the front, and the fodder is simply the two middle words.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone brazen shows no shame or embarrassment, which is exactly what being unembarrassed and bold without apology amounts to.

clue.text: Clobber heroin and ecstasy-injecting idiots

indicators.note: the idiots are doing the injecting, so the drugs go inside them

blocks.note: H is slang for heroin
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet
clots = fools

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline urging someone to beat up fools who shoot up drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' looks like a verb meaning hit; it is the British slang noun for gear or garments, and it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Clobber is British informal slang for the things you wear, your gear or outfit, so it stands for garments generally.

clue.text: Rogue with nothing on held naked monk on TV

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting one piece on another stacks it below the first
a naked word has been stripped of its outer covering, leaving only the core letters

blocks.note: a cad is a dishonourable man
FA as in 'sweet FA', British slang for nothing at all
the word held with its first and last letters stripped off

explanation.surface: A scandal story about a scoundrel caught undressed with a television cleric.
explanation.walkthrough: Brother Cadfael is the medieval monk-detective of Ellis Peters' novels, played by Derek Jacobi in the 1990s ITV series. 'Sweet FA' is a polite-ish British way of saying nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadfael is the Benedictine brother who solves murders in Shrewsbury Abbey in a British television drama series, so he is a small-screen cleric.

clue.text: Soppy language of drunkard overlooked by son

indicators.note: in a down entry, whatever overlooks a piece sits above it, so the son comes first

blocks.note: s = son, the genealogical abbreviation
a lush is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: The sentimental babble of a drunk, watched over by his embarrassed boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overlooked by' only works as a placing instruction because the clue is a down one: the son is above the drunkard.
explanation.definitionFit: Slush is mawkish, sentimental writing or talk, the gushing kind found in romantic novels, so it names soppy words.

clue.text: Large royal turned up comatose in rowdy boozer

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning a word up makes it read from the bottom, so the royal is written backwards

blocks.note: L = large, the clothing size
regal = royal
out cold, out for the count

explanation.surface: A hefty prince found unconscious in a noisy pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' tempts you towards a pub, which suits the surface; here it is a person who boozes. A lager lout is a young man who gets drunk on beer and turns aggressive.
explanation.definitionFit: A lager lout is the British term for a youth made loud and violent by drink, a heavy drinker who causes trouble.

clue.text: Those making punch have less of a hit?

definitions.text: Those making punch have less of a hit?

blocks.note: reads as bartenders mixing a bowl of fruit punch for a party
the setter means padded mitts that soften a blow, not a weaker drink

explanation.surface: Bar staff mixing a party punch that turns out rather weak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Punch' and 'hit' both lean towards drinks, a punch bowl and the kick of alcohol; both are really fist blows. The padding cushions each strike.
explanation.definitionFit: The padded mitts fighters wear are the equipment through which blows are thrown, and their cushioning reduces the impact of each strike.

clue.text: Men with energy flipping love horse and herb

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it end to end, so the love and the horse are written backwards together

blocks.note: OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
E = energy, the physics symbol
love = zero in tennis, shaped like O
a nag is an old horse

explanation.surface: Energetic lads who adore horses, and a sprinkle of something green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' could be a mild British expletive qualifying love; it is the instruction, and it turns the pair round as a unit.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregano is an aromatic plant of the mint family whose dried leaves flavour pizza and Mediterranean cooking, a standard kitchen example.

clue.text: Duke wearing a wig given smack?

blocks.note: D = duke, the peerage abbreviation
a rug is slang for a toupee, so someone wearing one is jokily 'rugged'

explanation.surface: A bewigged aristocrat receiving a slap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' looks like a blow to the duke's face; it is slang for heroin. The question mark flags both the definition by example and the made-up word for a wig-wearer.
explanation.definitionFit: Smack is street slang for heroin, so someone dosed with it has been sedated with narcotics, one example of that state.

clue.text: Treat this randy sap with abandon!

indicators.note: doing something with abandon means wildly and without restraint, so the letters are thrown about

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: An instruction to handle a lustful fool without inhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treat' opens the clue looking like a verb meaning handle; it is a noun, a sweet indulgence. A Danish pastry is a flaky, sweet breakfast bun.
explanation.definitionFit: A Danish pastry is a sweet flaky bun, often with fruit or custard, which counts as an indulgence or delicacy eaten as a reward.

clue.text: Popular spinster going topless around country

indicators.note: losing its top in an across clue means the spinster loses her first letter
turning around faces the shortened spinster the other way, so she is read backwards

blocks.note: in = fashionable, popular
a spinster is an old maid; MAID without its first letter

explanation.surface: A well-liked single woman sunbathing without a top as she tours abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The spinster has to become MAID before anything can be taken off her; 'around' then reverses what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: India is a large nation in South Asia, so it is a plain example of a sovereign state or nation.

clue.text: Architect chasing after common Aussie singer

indicators.note: something chasing another follows behind it, so the architect is placed second

blocks.note: a common is open public land, much like a heath
Sir Christopher Wren, who designed St Paul's Cathedral

explanation.surface: A designer pursuing a vulgar Australian pop star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' pushes you towards a pop star; it is a songbird. The heathwrens are small Australian ground-dwelling birds. 'Common' is a noun here, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Heathwrens are small brown songbirds native to Australian scrub and heathland, so an Australian songbird is a fair description.

clue.text: Doctor repelled by half-cut Thai's all-round thickness

indicators.note: something repelled is driven back the way it came, so the doctoring word runs backwards
cutting in half chops off two of the four letters of the nationality
by means next to, so the two pieces stand side by side

blocks.note: to doctor is to rig, to tamper with
the first half of the four-letter word

explanation.surface: A physician put off by a tipsy Thai man's substantial waistline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is the verb, not a medic, and 'half-cut' (British slang for drunk) is an instruction. The 's stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Girth is the measurement right round the middle of something, its circumference, so it is thickness measured all round.

clue.text: An outstanding bill from Italy?

blocks.note: reads as an unpaid invoice, money still owed
the setter means a prominent beak with a high bridge, of the kind seen on classical Latin statues

explanation.surface: An unpaid invoice arriving from an Italian creditor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' means protruding rather than unpaid, and 'bill' is a beak rather than a demand for payment. The question mark covers the loose geography.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman nose is one with a prominent, high, curved bridge, and a bill is a beak, so a jutting one fits.

clue.text: Awfully asocial American is very lewd

indicators.note: something done awfully is done badly, so the unsociable word's letters are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
US = American

explanation.surface: A standoffish American turns out to be thoroughly smutty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awfully' looks like it intensifies 'asocial'; it scrambles it instead, and the American is added after.
explanation.definitionFit: Salacious means having an excessive, indecent interest in sex, the same sense as obscene, smutty or lecherous.

clue.text: Hard drug consuming male, half-cut teen and fellow pupil

indicators.note: the drug consumes the male, taking him inside itself
half of the four-letter youngster is chopped off, keeping the front two

blocks.note: Class A is the UK legal category for the most dangerous drugs
M = male
the first half of the youngster

explanation.surface: A man and a tipsy teenager both on hard drugs, school friends together.
explanation.walkthrough: Class A is the British legal category of the most harmful drugs, such as heroin and cocaine. The man goes inside it before the letter A.
explanation.definitionFit: A classmate is someone taught in the same form at school, so another student sharing the room is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Perverted male loves impotent leaders

indicators.note: perverted means twisted out of its proper form, so the man's letters are rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters
duck is a northern English term of endearment, like love

explanation.surface: A kinky man is drawn to rulers who cannot perform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impotent' tempts you into the bedroom with the rest of the surface; it means powerless. A lame duck is an official serving out a term with no real authority left.
explanation.definitionFit: Lame ducks are office-holders, often outgoing presidents, whose power has drained away before they leave, so they are powerless rulers.

clue.text: Daily mass occasionally put on by grand yoga centres

indicators.note: only now and then, so every other letter of the weight word is kept
the grand is put onto the word in the sense of worked into it, slipped in among its letters

blocks.note: a daily is a cleaner who comes in every day; so is a char
the second and fourth letters of the four
a grand is a thousand, K

explanation.surface: Daily church service now and then, plus a big fancy set of meditation points.
explanation.walkthrough: A daily and a char are both British words for a cleaning woman. The thousand sits between the A and R of the cleaner, a loose placement the clue only hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: In yoga and Hindu tradition, chakras are the points of spiritual energy thought to lie along the spine, so they are energy centres.

clue.text: Top of tree was in need of treatment

indicators.note: something needing treatment is not yet in its proper state, so the letters must be reworked

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: The crown of a tree was diseased and needed a tree surgeon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top of tree' reads as one phrase about a branch tip; the definition is only 'Top', a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A top is any garment for the upper body, and a knitted pullover or jumper is one kind, so this defines by example.

clue.text: Drop of tequila in a vessel makes you misbehave

indicators.note: a single drop is the first small bit, so only the opening letter is taken
the drop goes in the vessel, placed inside it

blocks.note: a cup is a drinking vessel
the first letter of the spirit

explanation.surface: A shot of tequila in your glass gets you behaving badly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a warning about drink; the word 'a' belongs to the wordplay, joining the vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: To act up is a phrasal verb for behaving badly, especially of children or machines, the same meaning as being naughty.

clue.text: Clear French wine? Escort necks one with Charlie!

indicators.note: to neck is British slang for swallowing a drink fast, so the escort gulps the others down inside

blocks.note: vin is French for wine
a date is a companion for the evening
I = one, the Roman numeral
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A boozy night with a paid companion who downs drinks alongside the cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie is also slang for cocaine, which the surface leans on. 'Clear' is a verb here, as in clearing someone's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To vindicate someone is to prove them blameless and restore their reputation, which is clearing them of an accusation.

clue.text: One does wrong to bump off southern private

indicators.note: bumping off is killing, getting rid of, so the southern letter is removed

blocks.note: a sinner is one who does wrong
S = southern

explanation.surface: A wrongdoer sets out to murder a soldier from the South.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like an army rank beside the killing; it means personal, as in one's inner thoughts.
explanation.definitionFit: Inner feelings are private ones, kept within and not shown, so the adjective shares the sense of personal and hidden.

clue.text: Groups pinching American bottoms

indicators.note: to pinch something is to hold it tight between fingers, so the groups grip the American

blocks.note: sets = groups
A = American

explanation.surface: A gang of people groping American backsides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching bottoms' is a single saucy picture; 'bottoms' is detached to be the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Your seat is the part of the body you sit on, a polite word for the backside, so the plurals match.

clue.text: A couple of lines nurse gets funny man

blocks.note: used as it stands
L = line, twice
EN = enrolled nurse

explanation.surface: A nurse is handed a couple of lines to deliver in a comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Several comedians fit: Woody Allen, or the Irish comic Dave Allen, famous on British television. The enrolled nurse is an older British grade of nurse.
explanation.definitionFit: Woody Allen and Dave Allen were both celebrated comedians, so the surname stands for a comic by example.

clue.text: One cuddling a famous reverend

blocks.note: to spoon is to lie curled against a partner, one body fitted against the other
the Oxford warden whose muddled slips of the tongue gave a wordplay device his name

explanation.surface: A well-known vicar caught in an embrace.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rev William Spooner of New College, Oxford, was said to swap the starts of words, as in 'a well-boiled icicle'; crosswords still use the spoonerism.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who spoons is lying snugly close to a partner, and William Spooner was the clergyman remembered for transposed-sound gaffes.

clue.text: One behind promotion for a film?

blocks.note: someone who trails is lagging at the back of the field
the short preview of scenes screened before other features to drum up an audience

explanation.surface: Someone working behind the scenes on a movie's publicity campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One behind promotion' reads as the person responsible for the publicity; split it, and 'behind' means trailing.
explanation.definitionFit: A trailer is anyone who lags at the rear, and also the cinema preview of clips advertising a coming feature.

clue.text: Bones mostly associated with the head?

definitions.text: Bones mostly associated with the head?

blocks.clueFragment: Bones mostly associated with the head
blocks.note: reads as the skeleton, the skull being the set of bones most tied to the head
the setter means a doctor, from 'sawbones' and the Star Trek medic nicknamed Bones, one whose work is mostly on the brain

explanation.surface: A quiz about which bones belong mainly to the skull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bones' is slang for a doctor, from sawbones; this one works chiefly on the brain and nervous system, so 'the head' is where they operate.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist operating on the brain, spine and nerves is a medic whose work is largely concentrated inside the skull.
